title: Punched cards ran looms in 1804, long before they ran computers

cover.alt: A wooden loom in a museum, with a wide fan of yellow cords above it and a red cloth with a white patterned border being woven below.

body: Before 1804, weaving a complex pattern such as damask needed a second worker, the *draw boy*, to pull up the right warp threads by hand for every row. Joseph Marie Jacquard patented a device that sits on top of a loom and does it automatically, building on ideas from Basile Bouchon, Jean-Baptiste Falcon and Jacques Vaucanson. It reads a chain of **punched cards**, one card for each row of the design: where a card has a hole, a hook lifts its threads; where it doesn't, the hook stays put. Charles Babbage later borrowed the idea of swappable punched cards for his Analytical Engine.

slides.alt: A wooden loom works steadily: a wide fan of yellow cords above shifts as threads rise and fall, and a red cloth with a white patterned border grows below.
slides.caption: A Jacquard loom at work at De Museumfabriek in Enschede, Netherlands: the cords above lift threads for each row of a patterned red cloth.

slides.question: A loom head has 400 hooks, and each hook pulls 4 threads. How many warp threads can it control?
slides.explanation: 400 × 4 = 1,600 warp ends: a cloth 1,600 threads wide, with the design repeated four times across it.

events.text: Basile Bouchon guides a loom with a punched paper roll
Jean-Baptiste Falcon uses separate pasteboard cards
Joseph Marie Jacquard patents his machine
Computers replace the cards, steering thousands of hooks

slides.question: What did each punched card stand for?
slides.explanation: Each card held the holes for one row of the design, so the chain of cards was the pattern, row by row.
